# v2.72 — Training Tracker no longer runs as root

This stable release rolls up dev pre-releases v2.70-dev, v2.71-dev and v2.72-dev.

Until now the application process ran as **root** on every install. It doesn't any more. A web app that handles logins has no business running with full system privileges, and this release fixes that.

> ### ⚠️ Breaking change — one step to finish the upgrade
>
> **If you have automatic updates switched on**, there is nothing to do. Within about five minutes of updating, the server finishes the migration itself: it creates the service account, corrects file ownership, installs the update helper, and restarts the app so it comes back unprivileged. You can watch it happen in `/var/log/training-tracker/updates.log`.
>
> **If you do not**, run this once on the server after updating:
>
> ```bash
> bash /opt/training-tracker/deploy/install.sh
> ```
>
> Run it **as root**. On an LXC container you are normally root already; on a VM, prefix it with `sudo`.
>
> Until one of those two things happens, the in-app **"Update now"** button will refuse to run — it shows an error telling you exactly this — and the app keeps running as root, so you get none of the security benefit below. The script is safe to re-run, takes a few minutes, and leaves your database and settings untouched.
>
> Why it is needed at all: the updater performing the upgrade is the *old* one, from the release you are coming from. It knows nothing about service accounts, so it cannot set one up while installing the release that introduces them. Once you are on this version, every future update applies its own changes and this never arises again.

## What's new

**The app runs as a dedicated unprivileged account.** The installer creates a `training-tracker` system user with no login shell, and the service runs under it inside a sandboxed systemd unit — no special privileges, a restricted set of system calls, and a read-only view of the filesystem apart from its own directory. If the application is ever compromised, the attacker gets that account and not the machine.

**Updates still work, without granting the app any privilege at all.** The obvious way to let an unprivileged service restart itself is a `sudo` rule. We deliberately did not do that. Every mechanism of that shape — sudoers entries, setuid helpers, polkit rules — hands the service a way to become root, and every one depends on a package that may not be installed. Minimal LXC container templates frequently ship without `sudo` entirely, so a sudoers-based design would fail on exactly the platform this project is most often deployed to.

Instead, the app **asks**. It writes a small request file that it already owns; a privileged watcher notices, verifies the file really came from the app and is the right size and shape, and then matches its contents against three fixed instructions. Nothing else crosses that boundary — no filenames, no arguments — so there is nothing in it to tamper with. This needs no packages beyond what the system already has, and behaves identically on a container and a VM.

**Much less runs as root during an update.** Previously `npm install` ran as root on every update, which meant any package in the dependency tree could run installation scripts with full privileges. The dependency install, database migration, application build and database backup now all run as the unprivileged account. Only fetching the code and restarting the service still need root.

**The installer fails loudly.** It checks everything it depends on up front and lists *all* missing pieces at once, rather than getting half way through and stopping — or appearing to succeed and failing later in production. It also reports which account the app ended up running as, so a successful install visibly proves it is no longer root.

**Scheduled jobs are set up for you.** Automatic updates, report exports and the daily credential check are installed as standard system scheduled jobs, each running with the least privilege it needs. Changing the auto-update schedule in the app now just updates a setting. A missed auto-update window — if the server was asleep, for example — runs late the same day rather than being skipped entirely.

## Fixed

- Saving a backup schedule silently did nothing when the scheduler was unavailable or the account was not permitted to use it. It now tells you, instead of leaving you believing backups were scheduled when they were not.
- Update failures reported a generic "Server returned an error" instead of the actual reason. They now show what went wrong and, where applicable, the exact command to run. Errors that used to be discarded are recorded in the system log.
- Documented commands that assumed `sudo` was installed have been corrected — the same assumption this release exists to remove.
- The documented example for the credential-check scheduled job used an account that could never have read the configuration file, so it could not have worked as written.

## Notes

- Scheduled-job logs have moved from `/var/log/training-tracker-*.log` into a single `/var/log/training-tracker/` directory.
- If you have changed `PORT` to a value below 1024, an unprivileged service cannot bind it. Either grant the service that one capability in `deploy/training-tracker.service`, or leave the port alone and put a reverse proxy in front — which is the better arrangement in any case.
